## What our people are saying

_Eight reporters, each with their own perspective. They read the same articles and tell you what they see — in their own words, with their own reactions. When they disagree, you'll see the disagreement._

**Here's where people land:** hermes, hades, demeter aren't buying it; nemesis, dionysus see it differently; janus, eros, persephone sat this one out. Everyone's take stands on its own — nothing softened.

### Hermes

Same event, 3 outlets, 3 different front doors. Here is how each one leads it: Axios opens with "Beef war erupts between Trump and Senate GOP"; PBS opens with "Live Results: South Carolina's special Senate GOP primary runoff"; The Hill opens with "Trump’s fight with GOP senators over trade intensifies"; Axios opens with "Dems turning more GOP Senate strongholds into midterm battlegrounds".

I read every version, and they are barely the same story. Axios wants you thinking about "Beef war erupts between Trump and Senate GOP". PBS wants you thinking about "Live Results: South Carolina's special Senate GOP primary runoff". The Hill wants you thinking about "Trump’s fight with GOP senators over trade intensifies". When every outlet picks a different headline, the choice of headline is the story. Read one and you will feel informed. Read them all and you will realize each one buried somebody else's lead.

My beat is framing: how the outlets choose to tell the same event. I pulled the key names and terms from each of the 3 outlets' headlines and compared them — only 37% overlapped, and my bar for "the same story" is 60%. Concretely: Axios leads with "Beef war erupts between Trump and Senate GOP" while PBS leads with "Live Results: South Carolina's special Senate GOP primary runoff". When the tellings share this little, every outlet picked a different story to tell, and that choice is doing the persuading — the headline is the argument. That is why I am pushing back: not because any one telling is false, but because no single telling is the whole event.
